title: Chemistry Textbooks Have Been Wrong for Almost 100 Years!
summary:
Imagine your science textbook has been teaching you something wrong for almost 100 years. That's what a team of chemists just discovered about a basic idea in chemistry.

The idea is called the "inductive effect." It explains how atoms pull on electrons (tiny particles inside atoms) when they're connected in a molecule. Think of it like a tug-of-war. One atom pulls electrons toward itself, and that changes how the molecule behaves.

For decades, textbooks have said this pull travels through three or four bonds — like a chain of people passing a message down the line, getting weaker each time. But new research from Cardiff University and the University of Newcastle in Australia says that's not true. The pull actually stops after just one bond.

"The inductive effect does not extend beyond one bond," says Dr. Mark Elliott, the lead author. That's a huge change because chemists use this idea to explain why molecules act the way they do. If the old explanation was wrong, then other explanations built on it might need fixing too.

The scientists didn't do one big experiment. Instead, they gathered evidence from many studies already published and combined it with their own data. Some of that evidence was already out there — just not widely known.

This matters because organic chemistry helps us make medicines, plastics, and farming chemicals. If we understand molecules better, we can design better products. Already, two exam boards in the U.K. are reviewing how they teach this topic. So next time you open a chemistry book, remember: even textbooks can be wrong!
why_it_matters: It shows that even things printed in textbooks can be wrong, and that checking evidence and asking questions is how science gets better — a habit you can use in your own schoolwork.

Science textbooks get updated when new evidence shows an old explanation was wrong — just as doctors once had to learn that tiny germs cause disease.

Article_Structure: WHO: A team of chemists led by Dr. Mark Elliott at Cardiff University and the University of Newcastle in Australia.
WHAT: They found that the 'inductive effect' stops after just one bond, not three or four as textbooks have said for almost 100 years.
WHERE: Research from universities in the U.K. and Australia, now being reviewed by two exam boards in the U.K.
WHY: Because chemists have used the old explanation to understand molecules, so fixing it could change what students are taught and how new products are designed.

perspectives.description: They are glad the mistake is being corrected, because understanding molecules better can lead to better medicines, plastics and farm chemicals.
They point out that the team combined evidence from studies that already existed instead of running one big new experiment, so more proof would help.
They note that science often corrects itself slowly, and that textbooks and exams can take years to catch up with new discoveries.
